title: Endosymbiosis: Did Complex Life Begin with a Merger?
question: Why did the complex cells that make up animals, plants and fungi arise only once in four billion years, and why did it take a partnership between two different organisms?
summary: Every complex cell on Earth descends from a single ancient merger in which one microbe came to live inside another. That event may explain why complex life is so rare.
content:
For roughly two billion years, life on Earth consisted of bacteria and archaea: small, simple, endlessly inventive in chemistry but structurally modest. Then, once, a new kind of cell appeared: the eukaryote, with a nucleus, internal compartments and a vast genome. Every animal, plant, fungus and amoeba descends from that single event.

The Merger Hypothesis

Lynn Margulis argued in the 1960s that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria swallowed by a larger host and never digested. The evidence is now overwhelming: mitochondria have their own circular DNA, divide independently, have bacterial-style ribosomes, and their genes group with alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplasts trace to cyanobacteria. The host appears to have been an archaeon, related to the Asgard archaea.

Why Energy Is the Bottleneck

Bacteria generate energy across their outer membrane, so as a cell grows, its surface area falls behind its volume. Eukaryotes escaped this by internalising the membranes: each mitochondrion keeps a tiny genome to regulate its own power station locally. Nick Lane estimates that per gene, a eukaryotic cell can spend thousands of times more energy than a bacterium. That surplus pays for large genomes, complex regulation, and eventually multicellular bodies.

Why Only Once?

Bacteria have been swallowing each other for billions of years, yet only one merger became a stable, heritable partnership that scaled. The barrier may be the tangled transition: host and symbiont must become mutually dependent, genes must migrate to the host nucleus, and a protein-import system must evolve. If so, complex life is not an inevitable climb up a ladder but a rare, contingent fusion. That has direct consequences for how common we expect complex life to be elsewhere.

The Order of Events

The old picture had a nucleated cell first, which then acquired mitochondria. Many researchers now favour mitochondria early, perhaps triggering the evolution of the nucleus and the cell's internal architecture. The truth is still contested, and genomics keeps shifting the picture.

perspectives.title: Evolutionary Biology
perspectives.description: Symbiosis is a creative force, not just an exception. Major transitions in evolution often involve formerly independent entities merging into a new individual, with conflict suppressed by shared fate.

perspectives.title: Bioenergetics
perspectives.description: The key is energy per gene. Mitochondria let cells decouple size and genome complexity from the limits of a single energy-producing membrane.

perspectives.title: Astrobiology
perspectives.description: If the eukaryotic merger was a freak accident, microbes may be common in the universe while complex life is vanishingly rare.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Biology
perspectives.description: What counts as an individual organism if each of our cells is a chimera? Individuality looks like a stable negotiation rather than a fixed fact.

connections: Cooperation and the evolution of altruism
openQuestions: What was the host cell, and did it already have a complex interior before mitochondria arrived?
Why has no second endosymbiosis of this scale produced another lineage of complex cells?
Was the merger driven by metabolic exchange, defence, or an accident of predation?
Does the rarity of this step explain the Fermi paradox?
